name: Rouge
lede: Rouge is the French word for red, which English borrowed for the red powders and creams of the face and for the fine red polish of jewellers; the deep, slightly cool red on this page is the shade the word now names.

sections.title: A French word in an English mouth
sections.body:
*Rouge* is simply "red" in French, and in French it is the ordinary word for the color, not a special one [1][2]. Latin had a solid basic term for red, *ruber*, with a frequent doublet *rubeus*, and a rich supplementary vocabulary of reds beside them, which is the stock the French word descends from [1]. In the thirteenth century it became interchangeable with *escarlate*, the name of a costly cloth that happened to be nearly always red, and the other Romance languages followed with their own forms of scarlet [2]. In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries French even used *rouge* as an intensifier, much as we use "very", so that a tall man could be "rouge grand" [3].

English kept the French word for two narrow jobs: the red that colors the face, and the red powder that polishes metal [4]. Paterson's dictionary records both, as a powder used by jewellers and as the make-up used to redden the cheeks, often made from carmine [4]. The color name as a color, a deep strong red, is a later and thinner use: Maerz and Paul record it from 1839, and the swatch here is the screen version that Wikipedia and the xkcd survey use [5].

That thinness is the honest state of the record. The name has no pigment of its own behind it, and the color books mostly mention rouge in passing, as a cosmetic, a polish, a slogan or a place [2][4][9]. This article therefore follows the thing the word was attached to most often, the red on the face, then the red polish, then the political red, and keeps the swatch for the end [4][9][13].

sections.title: Red for the face
sections.body:
Medieval clerics and moralists condemned make-up on high-born women, because to the Church it falsified what God had made [6]. Pastoureau notes that a light red on the cheeks was sometimes tolerated as a sign of modesty, while red lips were condemned as an abomination that made a woman a witch or a prostitute [6]. Romances of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries still prized the contrast of white skin with red cheeks and lips [6].

New World cochineal changed the economics of the cosmetic [7]. Within a few years of the Conquest the Spanish had taken over the Mexican cochineal industry, and Finlay reports that in 1575 alone about 80 metric tons reached Spain [7]. Women wanted it as the ultimate cosmetic [7]. Finlay reads a line in *Twelfth Night*, in which Olivia says her portrait's red is "in grain", as a joke on the dye's name and the idea of a color that is ingrained [7]. Venice became the great market for red, and Finlay quotes Jan Morris for the figure that around 1700 the city held 2,508 nuns and 11,654 prostitutes: no wonder, he says, there was a market for rouge [7].

Rouge was not always from insects. Field in 1835 lists *rouge*, *rouge végétale*, Chinese rouge and pink saucers together as preparations of safflower [8]. Tingry in 1804 describes cosmetic rouge made from the mineral talc, here called Briançon chalk, as a base with carmine [8]. The modern dictionary still lists the red powder made from safflower under the same word [4].

sections.title: The painted court
sections.body:
The French court of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries took the habit further than any earlier society, by Pastoureau's account [9]. Faces were whitened with ceruse, a lead white, and then marked in red at the lips and cheekbones with products based on cinnabar or lead oxide mixed into beeswax, mutton fat or vegetable oils [9]. Both bases were poisons, as was the arsenic that some courtiers took in lozenges to pale the skin further [9]. The toxicity of ceruse was beginning to be recognised, but concern for appearances outweighed the risk [9].

In courtly society red was nearly obligatory, and the higher the rank, the more vivid it had to be [9]. The red became so closely tied to rank that "red" itself came to mean make-up, and someone who withdrew to the country was said to have "quit the red" [9]. When the young Marie-Antoinette arrived at Versailles in 1770 she was disconcerted by all the painted faces, and by then make-up at court was already declining [9].

The cosmetic did not vanish. About 1780 Paris advertisements still praised a *rouge de la reine* ("queen's red", though which queen is unclear) and an "entirely vegetal", non-toxic red sold by a Demoiselle Latour [9]. In the nineteenth century heavy rouge came to belong to women on the margins of society, and painters such as Manet and Toulouse-Lautrec made pictures of them [9].

sections.title: Lipstick and the names of red
sections.body:
After the First World War lip color became an article of mass consumption, sold in tubes with a turning mechanism and in a great number of shades [9]. Pastoureau observes that the names changed too: from plain words such as carmine, garnet, cherry, vermilion and poppy to catchy phrases meant to create intrigue rather than name the exact color [9]. Makeup testers turned the counter into what he calls a dictionary of red [9].

The turning point he identifies is 1927, when the chemist Paul Baudecroux invented an indelible, eosin-based red for lips and sold it as *Rouge Baiser*, "red kiss" [9]. It was a hit into the 1950s, and the name is still used for a range of cosmetics today [9]. Greenfield adds that cochineal extract, carmine, is still in lipstick and rouge, along with candy, yogurt and Campari [10].

Compare the neighbors: [[carmine]], [[crimson]] and [[lipstick-red]] are the same family of cool, strong reds, and [[scarlet]] is the warmer one [11].

sections.title: Jeweller's rouge
sections.body:
The other rouge is a polish. Jeweller's rouge is a very fine powder of red iron oxide, also called colcothar, Crocus Martis and Venetian red [4]. Its particles are non-abrasive, which makes it good for polishing gold and silver [8]. In the same family of iron-oxide reds the Compendium lists Persian red, Indian red and caput mortuum, which are generally synthetic [8].

Finlay tells a small story of the polish from Whitby, where jet was carved and polished for mourning jewellery [12]. The workers were nicknamed "red devils", and a modern jeweller, Hal Redvers-Jones, worked out why when he found a rusty cocoa tin of rouge in a derelict workshop and a jug for mixing it with oil [12]. His explanation, that the wet red polish sprayed around the workshop and splattered the workers' smocks, faces and hair, is a reconstruction and not a record [12]. It is a good case of a color being the by-product of a trade.

sections.title: A political red
sections.body:
In France the word acquired a politics [13]. The red cap of the Revolution, the *bonnet rouge*, appeared in 1789 and was the emblem of the sans-culottes, and in 1792 the mob forced the king to wear one [13]. Greenfield points out that this proletarian red could be made with cheap French madder, where the aristocrat's red had been foreign cochineal [14]. By the 1840s "un rouge" meant a person of the most progressive political ideas, and later a revolutionary [13]. At the turn of the twentieth century the "red unions" were set against the "yellow" ones that rejected strikes [15].

One piece of lore needs correcting. The red heels, *talons rouges*, of the French aristocracy are often put down to the Duke of Orléans, who is supposed to have been short; Pastoureau treats this as a legend, and dates the fashion to Versailles in the 1670s and 1680s [13]. For more on the family, see [[red]], [[vermilion]] and [[madder]].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch, `#AB1239`, is a vivid red in the 1955 ISCC-NBS system, 6.0 units from the center of that block [5]. A near-duplicate in our library is Wikipedia's Vivid Burgundy, 2.4 units away [5]. Because the word means plain red and also names a make-up and a polish, no one shade is the rouge [4]. Historical rouge was whatever red the maker could get: cinnabar, cochineal, safflower, carmine or iron oxide [4][8][9]. The nearest of our named colors is [[raspberry]], at 5.1 units [5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Very few paintings in our archive of 23,781 hold this red over a large part of the canvas [16]. A color within six units of the swatch covers at least five per cent of the picture in only 7 works [16]. The largest covers are Alonso Cano's *The crucified Christ appears to Saint Teresa of Avila* (1629, 24 per cent), Matisse's [[painting:smk-KMSr81|Nude with a White Scarf]] (1909, 20 per cent), Kirchner's *Two Girls under an Umbrella* (1910) and Juan de Flandes's *The Baptism of Christ* (1508) [16]. The list also includes a *Holy Family* attributed to Caravaggio (1603, 9 per cent) [16]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so read the matches as screen colors, not as identifications of pigment [16].

Inside a painting the color usually plays an accent, which is what a deep rouge-like red does in a robe or a cheek [16]. In printed English the word *rouge* rises from about a fifth of its eventual peak in 1800 to nearly 90 per cent by 1940, and peaks around 1990, though Google Books counts every use of the word, including names such as Moulin Rouge [17]. Westland notes that Moulin Rouge was one of the hot colors on American muscle cars in 1970 [18].
